video.title: Why Pros Hit So Far Away

classification.reason: The coach provides executable drills and cues, such as holding a cone or weight in the non-hitting hand and using a lunging restriction drill to calibrate lateral contact spacing.

problem.title_as_question: Why do pros hit so far away from their body on the forehand?
problem.definition: Improving forehand mechanics requires pushing the contact point farther away laterally and in depth, but players habitually revert to a jammed contact lane that restricts the shoulder and trunk rotation.
prerequisites: closed or semi-open stance unit turn
problem.target_player: intermediate players working on modern forehand mechanics who struggle with crowding the ball

symptoms.description: The hitting arm crunches in close to the torso like a chicken wing or gets pinned behind the rotating trunk.
The player underhand yanks the elbow across the torso instead of driving it forward along the pressing vector.
Body balance falls off to the left onto the back heel during the follow-through instead of driving through the court.

causes.statement: Players intuitively regress to an old, crowded contact lane developed from pushing mechanics instead of trusting lateral distance.
The non-hitting arm dangles loosely instead of extending across the body to calibrate spacing and stabilize trunk rotation.
Crowding the ball deprives the hitting arm apparatus of room, forcing the elbow to yank across the torso rather than pressing forward.
Players fail to budget additional depth buffer in front when stepping or leaning forward, crashing into the ball.

angles.summary: Pushing the ball far away laterally enables the pressing vector where the hitting elbow drives straight forward along the chest's facing orientation.
Demonstrating hits with a dangling left arm versus an extended left arm highlights loss of trunk coordination and velocity when the non-hitting side is loose.
Proper modern lateral spacing feels comically far to the outside compared to the familiar jammed recreational hitting lane.
Vertical margin comes from tilting the entire trunk plane of rotation on low balls rather than independently lifting with the arm.

solutions.summary: Push the non-hitting arm across the body during preparation to serve as an active spacing marker and stabilizer.
Hold an object like a cone in the non-hitting hand during preparation so peripheral vision keeps the brain aware of that balance lever.
solutions.external_goal: Hold a cone in the non-hitting hand

solutions.summary: Upgrade from holding a cone to holding a 2.5 lb weight in the non-hitting hand to add visceral load to the stabilizing side.
solutions.external_goal: Hold a 2.5 lb weight in the non-hitting hand

solutions.summary: Execute the lunge drill by restricting adjustment footwork to a single lunge to force contact into a wide lateral slot and find optimal shoulder release.
solutions.external_goal: Take as few steps as possible and lunge to reach the feed

solutions.summary: Stay patient and wait for the ball into the proper depth slot rather than overreaching forward with the racket and sticking the hips back.
